output.title: Cell-based bookings in three regions
output.description: An invented travel company, Tidewater Travel. DNS spreads travellers across three active regions; each region hashes customers to two cells that share nothing on the request path. DynamoDB global tables replicate every booking, so a region can go dark and a bad deploy stays in one cell.

annotations.text: A cell is a complete, fixed-size copy of the booking stack. Requests never cross cells or regions; only data replicates.

simulations.title: us-east-1 goes dark
simulations.description: Five seconds in, us-east-1's load balancer stops answering. DNS health checks send its travellers to the other two regions, whose cells were sized to absorb one region's share. Bookings keep flowing; the region returns at 18 s.

action.text: Three regions take bookings. Each region splits customers across two cells; no request ever leaves its cell.
us-east-1 goes dark. DNS health checks stop sending travellers there within one check.
us-west-2 takes half of the extra traffic. Its cells run hotter but stay under capacity: that headroom is the design.
eu-west-1 takes the other half, with the same headroom.
us-east-1 is back and DNS sends its share home. Global tables replicated every booking while it was away.

simulations.title: A bad deploy stays in one cell
simulations.description: The release pipeline deploys to one canary cell first. The new build fails most bookings, but only in Cell 1 of us-east-1: about a sixth of traffic. The cell's alarm stops the rollout and rolls it back at 12 s.

action.text: Six cells, each a complete copy of the booking stack. The release pipeline deploys to one cell at a time, starting here.
Build 7.3 reaches the canary cell and fails most of its bookings.
Only that cell's customers notice. The neighbouring cell, and the four cells in the other regions, carry on untouched.
The cell's CloudWatch alarm halts the rollout and rolls it back. Bookings succeed again.

expectations.label: The bad build fails bookings in its cell
